analysis.one_liner: Removes fracking's exemption from federal drinking-water law and requires disclosure of injected chemicals.
analysis.headline: The FRAC Act was referred to the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee the day it was introduced and never received a hearing, markup, or vote before Congress ended in January 2021.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would end the exemption that keeps oil and gas fracking outside the Safe Drinking Water Act, letting the EPA regulate fracking wells the way it regulates other underground injection. It would require companies to list the chemicals they plan to pump into the ground before drilling starts and what they actually used afterward, posted publicly on a searchable government website. If a first responder or doctor needs to know a chemical's identity to treat a patient, the company would have to hand it over even if it is a trade secret.
analysis.who_benefits: People who live near fracking wells and draw drinking water from the same groundwater; first responders and health care practitioners who currently cannot get the chemical identity of a trade-secret substance without paperwork; and state or federal regulators who would gain information about what is being injected.

how_it_helps.text: The bill strikes the definition that excludes fracking from 'underground injection' under the Safe Drinking Water Act, so EPA's underground injection program would cover fracking wells for the first time since the 2005 exemption [S2] [S3].

Operators must disclose, before fracking begins, every chemical and proppant intended for use — with chemical identifiers, safety data sheets, and amounts — and again after operations, listing what was actually used [S2] [S3].
States or EPA must post all disclosures on a single, searchable public website [S3].

If a first responder or health care practitioner determines a trade-secret chemical identity is needed for diagnosis, treatment, or emergency response, the operator must disclose it immediately, regardless of any confidentiality agreement [S2] [S3].

States could take over enforcement of fracking rules on their own without assuming responsibility for every other kind of injection well, which lowers the practical barrier for state oversight [S2] [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Oil and gas producers and the service companies that formulate fracking fluids, who would face permitting requirements under federal drinking-water rules, would lose blanket trade-secret protection for fluid formulas (though core proprietary formulas still would not be publicly disclosed), and would bear record-keeping and compliance costs. Some of those costs could flow to consumers through energy prices and to landowners through lease terms.

drawbacks.text: Fracking is already regulated state by state, and many major producing states require chemical disclosure through voluntary or mandatory registries, so critics argue a federal layer adds cost without clear added safety [S3].
Compliance, permitting, and record-keeping costs would fall on oil and gas operators and could be passed to consumers through higher energy prices; the bill does not include a cost analysis [S3].

The bill preserves trade-secret protection for proprietary formulas from public disclosure, so the public website would still omit some specific identities; it only guarantees disclosure to medical and emergency personnel on request [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The public benefit is information and a legal handle: communities near wells would learn what is being injected, and emergency personnel could get a chemical's identity in time to matter, which is cheap to provide and potentially lifesaving. The real costs fall on operators as compliance and possible permitting burdens, and a fair objection is that states already do much of this. The bill is a modest, targeted transparency measure rather than a ban, and its main honest weakness is duplication with existing state disclosure programs.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee on the day it was introduced, the committee never acted on it, and it died when the 116th Congress ended in January 2021.

narrative.text: Sen. Bob Casey introduced the bill on December 17, 2019, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Environment and Public Works that same day [S5].
No further action was ever recorded: no hearing, no committee markup, no floor vote, in either chamber [S5].
Five Democratic senators cosponsored the bill; no Republican signed on [S4].
The 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021, and the bill expired with it [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Oil and gas operators kept their Safe Drinking Water Act exemption and their existing trade-secret protections for fracking fluid formulas, and no federal chemical-disclosure requirement was created.

for.name: Sen. Bob Casey
for.role: Sponsor; introduced the bill and referred it to Environment and Public Works

against.name: Senate Environment and Public Works Committee
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by a Republican, in a Republican-led Senate
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill — no hearing, no markup, no vote — for the remainder of the Congress

against.name: Oil and gas industry
against.role: Major regulated industry with a strong stake in the existing exemption
against.what_they_did: Historically opposed federal Safe Drinking Water Act regulation of fracking, which the 2005 exemption it relied on reflected

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and all five cosponsors were Democrats, and the Republican-led Senate committee never brought the bill to a hearing or vote.

industries.note: The bill would strip the industry's 2005 exemption from Safe Drinking Water Act underground-injection rules and require it to document and disclose what it pumps into wells. Its interest in keeping the exemption runs directly against the interest of neighbors in knowing what is being injected near their water.

Formulators would face disclosure duties for constituents and would lose the practical leverage of trade secrets against doctors and first responders, though core proprietary formulas still would not be published. Suppliers benefit today from keeping fluid recipes confidential.
